An Algorithm for Discriminating the Complete Multiplicities of a Parametric Univariate Polynomial

Simin Qin Affiliation: HCIC–School of Mathematical Sciences, Center for Applied Mathematics of Guangxi, Guangxi Minzu University, Nanning 530006, China    Bican Xia Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Peking University, Beijing 100091, China    Jing Yang ††thanks: Corresponding author: yangjing0930@gmail.com. Affiliation: HCIC–School of Mathematical Sciences, Center for Applied Mathematics of Guangxi, Guangxi Minzu University, Nanning 530006, China
Abstract

In this paper, we tackle the parametric complete multiplicity problem for a univariate polynomial. Our approach to the parametric complete multiplicity problem has a significant difference from the classical method, which relies on repeated gcd computation. Instead, we introduce a novel technique that uses incremental gcds of the given polynomial and its high-order derivatives. This approach, formulated as non-nested subresultants, sidesteps the exponential expansion of polynomial degrees in the generated condition. We also uncover the hidden structure between the incremental gcds and pseudo-remainders. Our analysis reveals that the conditions produced by our new algorithm are simpler than those generated by the classical approach in most cases. Experiments show that our algorithm is faster than the one based on repeated gcd computation for problems with relatively big size.

1 Introduction

Solving univariate polynomials for roots is a very fundamental problem in computer algebra with numerous applications. Depending on whether the coefficients contain indeterminates, we categorize the problem into two sub-problems.

  • •

    For polynomials with constant coefficients, “solving” means finding/isolating the roots.

  • •

    For polynomials with parametric coefficients, “solving” means classifying the complete root structures the given polynomial may have and providing a set of conditions under which each structure occurs. By complete root structure, we mean the numbers of real and imaginary roots and their multiplicities. Thus complete root structure is also called complete multiplicity structure.

In this paper, we tackle the second problem. More explicitly, we consider a polynomial of the form P=an​xn+⋯+a0P=a_{n}x^{n}+\cdots+a_{0}, where an≠0a_{n}\neq 0 and aia_{i}’s are parameters which take values over the real field ℝ\mathbb{R}, and explore the problem of determining a set of conditions on aia_{i}’s (which provides a partition of the parameter set) so that PP exhibits a specific complete multiplicity structure under each condition. For instance, we consider a quartic polynomial P=a4​x4+a3​x3+a2​x2+a1​x+a0P=a_{4}x^{4}+a_{3}x^{3}+a_{2}x^{2}+a_{1}x+a_{0}, where a4≠0a_{4}\neq 0 and aia_{i}’s are real parameters. All the potential complete multiplicity structures of PP are:

((1,1,1,1),()),((1,1),(1,1)),((2,1,1),()),((2),(1,1)),((2,2),()),(();(2,2)),((3,1),()),((4),()),\begin{array}[]{llll}\left((1,1,1,1);()\right),&\left((1,1);(1,1)\right),&\left((2,1,1);()\right),&\left((2);(1,1)\right),\\ \left((2,2);()\right),&\left(();(2,2)\right),&\left((3,1);()\right),&\left((4);()\right),\end{array}

where (𝝁𝑹;𝝁𝑰)(\boldsymbol{\mu_{R}};\boldsymbol{\mu_{I}}) with #​𝝁𝑹+#​𝝁𝑰=n\#\boldsymbol{\mu_{R}}+\#\boldsymbol{\mu_{I}}=n is interpreted as follows:

  • •

    the real roots of PP have the multiplicity structure 𝝁𝑹\boldsymbol{\mu_{R}}, and

  • •

    the imaginary roots of PP have the multiplicity structure 𝝁𝑰\boldsymbol{\mu_{I}}.

For instance, if PP has a complete multiplicity structure ((2);(1,1))((2);(1,1)), then PP has a double real root and a pair of simple imaginary roots. With this setting, we aim to find a set of conditions C0,C1,…C_{0},C_{1},\ldots on aia_{i}’s so that

the complete multiplicity structure of P={((1,1,1,1);())iff C0 holds((1,1);(1,1))iff C1 holds⋮⋮((4);())iff C7 holds\text{the complete multiplicity structure of $P$}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}((1,1,1,1);())&\text{iff $C_{0}$ holds}\\ ((1,1);(1,1))&\text{iff $C_{1}$ holds}\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ ((4);())&\text{iff $C_{7}$ holds}\end{array}\right.

In general, the problem is stated as follows:

Problem: For every 𝝁𝒄=(𝝁𝑹;𝝁𝑰)\boldsymbol{\mu_{c}}=\left(\boldsymbol{\mu_{R}};\boldsymbol{\mu_{I}}\right) where 𝝁𝑹=(μR,1,…,μR,m1)\boldsymbol{\mu_{R}}=(\mu_{R,1},\ldots,\mu_{R,m_{1}}) and 𝝁𝑰=(μI,1,…,μI,m2)\boldsymbol{\mu_{I}}=(\mu_{I,1},\ldots,\mu_{I,m_{2}}) are such that

  • •

    μR,1≥…≥μR,m1>0\mu_{R,1}\geq\ldots\geq\mu_{R,m_{1}}>0,

  • •

    μI,1=μI,2≥…≥μI,m2−1=μI,m2>0\mu_{I,1}=\mu_{I,2}\geq\ldots\geq\mu_{I,m_{2}-1}=\mu_{I,m_{2}}>0, and

  • •

    ∑i=1m1μR,i+∑i=1m2μI,i=n,\sum_{i=1}^{m_{1}}\mu_{R,i}+\sum_{i=1}^{m_{2}}\mu_{I,i}=n,

find a necessary and sufficient condition on the coefficients of a polynomial PP over ℝ\mathbb{R} of degree nn such that the complete multiplicity structure of PP is 𝝁𝒄\boldsymbol{\mu_{c}}.

This problem is significant as it has numerous applications in various fields, such as mathematics, science, and engineering. Due to its importance, the problem and several related problems have already been extensively studied (e.g., see [3, 6, 10, 11, 12, 15]). In [15], Yang, Hou and Zeng gave an algorithm to generate a condition for discriminating different complete multiplicity structures of a univariate polynomial (referred to as YHZ’s condition hereinafter) by making use of repeated gcd computation for parametric polynomials [1, 2, 13]. A similar idea was adopted by Gonzalez-Vega et al. [3] for solving the real root classification and quantifier elimination problems by using Sturm-Habicht sequences. Roughly speaking, this method computes multiple factors at different levels, which can be realized by repeated gcd computation, i.e., computing the gcd of PP and its first derivative, the gcd of the previous gcd and its derivative, and so on. For the gcd at each level, we determine the condition that it has a certain number of distinct real roots/pairs of imaginary roots. By conjoining all the conditions at different levels, one can get a condition that PP has a given complete multiplicity structure. It should be pointed out that in YHZ’s method, the polynomials in the conditions are computed from repeated gcds whose coefficients are nested determinants. Thus, the “size” of these polynomials increases dramatically when the degree of PP grows, causing a huge computational burden.

A coarser version of the problem, which is stated as the parametric multiplicity problem, has been well studied (mainly via repeated gcd computation) in classical subresultant theory (e.g., [16]). In the parametric multiplicity structure, we do not differentiate real and imaginary roots, and thus, the multiplicity structure considered is called a complex multiplicity structure. Recently, Hong and Yang revisited the problem in [5, 8], resulting in two non-nested conditions for determining the multiplicity structure. It is shown that the generated conditions by [5, 8] are smaller than that produced via repeated gcd computation. Note that the complete multiplicity can be viewed as the refinement of complex multiplicity. We aim to find conditions with “small” size for the complete multiplicity problem, measured in terms of the number of polynomials appearing in the conditions and their maximum degree.

The main contribution of this paper is to provide such a condition, which has a smaller size than that in the previous methods. The key idea for generating the new condition is to replace the repeated gcds with the gcds of PP and its high-order derivatives of different orders for describing the multiple factors at different levels. For this purpose, we introduce the concept of incremental gcd and prove that it can be written as some specific subresultant of PP and its derivatives (see Theorem 16). Then, we devise an algorithm for computing the condition for every possible complete multiplicity structure PP may have. It is shown that the output condition has a smaller number of polynomials, and the maximal degree of polynomials in the condition is also significantly smaller than those in YHZ’s method. Furthermore, we also explore the relationship among these incremental gcds and identify an interesting structure (see Proposition 20) which is similar to the generalized Habicht’s theorem in [7].

The paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we first present the problem to be addressed in a formal way. In Section 3, we review the concept of subresultant for multiple polynomials and its equivalent form in roots. In Section 4, we present the main result of the paper (Theorem 16), which is followed by a detailed proof in Section 5. In Section 6, we design an algorithm for solving the proposed problem with the newly developed tool. In Section 7, we compare the performance of the algorithm and the size of polynomials output by the algorithm and those given by previous works. To keep the presentation of the main result in a tight manner, we postpone the proofs for two secondary results (which we hope could be useful for tackling other related problems) to Appendices A and B.

3 Preliminaries

A useful tool for formulating the multiple factors of a polynomial is subresultant for multiple polynomials, which is proposed by Hong and Yang in [6, 7] with several variants developed in [14] and is usually defined in the form of determinant polynomial.

Definition 6 (Determinant polynomial).

Let 𝐌\boldsymbol{M} be a p×qp\times q matrix where p≤qp\leq q. Then the determinant polynomial of 𝐌\boldsymbol{M}, written as dp𝐌\operatorname*{dp}\boldsymbol{M}, is defined as

dp𝑴=∑i=0q−p𝑴(i)​xi\operatorname*{dp}\boldsymbol{M}=\sum_{i=0}^{q-p}\boldsymbol{M}^{(i)}x^{i}

where 𝐌(i)=|𝐌1,…,𝐌p−1,𝐌q−i|\boldsymbol{M}^{(i)}=\left|\boldsymbol{M}_{1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{M}_{p-1},\boldsymbol{M}_{q-i}\right| and 𝐌k\boldsymbol{M}_{k} stands for the kk-th column of 𝐌\boldsymbol{M}.

4 Main Results

Definition 14 (Conjugate).

Let 𝛍=(μ1,…,μm)∈ℳ⁡(n)\boldsymbol{\mu}=(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{m})\in\mathcal{M}(n). Then the conjugate of 𝛍\boldsymbol{\mu} is defined by 𝛍¯=(μ¯1,…,μ¯n)\boldsymbol{\bar{\mu}}=(\bar{\mu}_{1},\dots,\bar{\mu}_{n}) where

μ¯i=#⁡{j∈[1,…,m]:μj≥i}.\bar{\mu}_{i}=\#\{j\in[1,\dots,m]:\mu_{j}\geq i\}.
Definition 15 (Incremental gcd).

Given 𝐅\boldsymbol{F} as in Notation 7, let

Gi=gcd⁡(F0,F1,…,Fi).G_{i}=\gcd(F_{0},F_{1},\ldots,F_{i}).

Given P∈ℝ⁡[x]P\in\mathbb{R}[x] of degree nn with mult(P)=𝛍\operatorname*{mult}(P)=\boldsymbol{\mu}, assume 𝛍¯=(μ¯1,…,μ¯n)\boldsymbol{\bar{\mu}}=(\bar{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\bar{\mu}_{n}). where

Gi=R(μ¯1,…,μ¯i)​(P(0),P(1),…,P(i))G_{i}=R_{(\bar{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\bar{\mu}_{i})}\big(P^{(0)},P^{(1)},\ldots,P^{(i)}\big)

One may wonder whether there are inherent relationships among R𝜹​(𝑭)R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}(\boldsymbol{F})’s. Indeed, we succeed to find such a relationship for polynomials with formal coefficients, which reveals the hidden structures in the potential GiG_{i}’s and converts the computation of subresultants into that of pseudo-remainders. We hope this relationship could be useful for exploring more hidden structures among the potential GiG_{i}’s and can be applied to enhance the efficiency of computing R𝜹​(𝑭)R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}(\boldsymbol{F})’s. The proof of the proposition can be found in Appendix A.

5 Proof of Theorem 16

This section is devoted to proving the paper’s main result (Theorem 16). To achieve this goal, we first rewrite R𝜹​(𝑭)R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}(\boldsymbol{F}) from an expression in coefficients to that in multiple roots through divided difference. Then we simplify the resulting expression in roots with the multiplicity information (i.e., the evaluation of the kk-th derivative of PP at its multiple root rir_{i} is zero for 0≤k≤μi−10\leq k\leq\mu_{i}-1 and is nonzero when k=μik=\mu_{i} where μi\mu_{i} is the multiplicity of rir_{i}). It turns out that the simplified expression corresponds to a certain gcd in icgcd⁡𝑭\operatorname{icgcd}\boldsymbol{F}.

5.2 Property of confluent Vandermonde matrices

It is seen in Lemma 22 that the numer of the expression R𝜹​(𝑭)R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}(\boldsymbol{F}) in multiple roots is a generalization of the confluent Vandermonde matrix, which inspires us to consider this particular type of matrices.

Let pp and qq be positive integers. The p×qp\times q Vandermonde block in terms of xx is defined as

𝑼⁡(x,p,q)=(ci​j)1≤i≤p1≤j≤q\boldsymbol{U}(x;p,q)=(c_{ij})_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i\leq p\\ 1\leq j\leq q\end{subarray}}

where ci​j=(i−1j−1)​xi−jc_{ij}=\binom{i-1}{j-1}x^{i-j} with the convention (i−1j−1):=0\binom{i-1}{j-1}:=0 for i<ji<j.

Given 𝐱=(x1,…,xℓ)\boldsymbol{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{\ell}) and 𝛕=(τ1,…,τℓ)\boldsymbol{\tau}=(\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{\ell}), the 𝛕\boldsymbol{\tau}-confluent Vandermonde matrix in terms of 𝐱\boldsymbol{x} is defined as the k×k{k}\times{k} matrix

𝑽⁡(𝒙,𝝉):=[𝑼⁡(x1,k,τ1)⋯𝑼⁡(xℓ,k,τℓ)]\boldsymbol{V}(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\tau}):=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{U}(x_{1};{k},\tau_{1})&\cdots&\boldsymbol{U}(x_{\ell};{k},\tau_{\ell})\end{bmatrix}

where k=τ1+⋯+τℓ{k}=\tau_{1}+\cdots+\tau_{\ell} and 𝐔⁡(xi,k,τi)\boldsymbol{U}(x_{i};{k},\tau_{i}) is the k×τi{k}\times\tau_{i} Vandermonde block in terms of xix_{i}.

6 Algorithm

In order to design an algorithm to compute the conditions for discriminating all the potential complete multiplicities PP may have, we need two more tools developed by Hong et al., which are non-nested multiplicity discriminant [8] and discriminant sequence [15].

6.1 Non-nested multiplicity discriminants for univariate polynomials

Definition 27 (𝝀\boldsymbol{\lambda}-discriminant).

Let P=∑i=0nai​xi∈ℝ⁡[x]P=\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_{i}x^{i}\in\mathbb{R}[x] where an≠0a_{n}\neq 0 and 𝐅=(P(0)𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸,\boldsymbol{F}=(P^{(0)}, 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁P(1),…,P(n))P^{(1)},\ldots,P^{(n)}) and 𝛌∈ℳ⁡(n)\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\mathcal{M}(n). Then we call R𝛌​(𝐅)R_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}(\boldsymbol{F}) the 𝝀\boldsymbol{\lambda}-discriminant of PP.

Theorem 28 (​​[8]).

We have

mult(P)=𝝁⟺𝝁¯=max𝝀∈ℳ⁡(n)R𝝀​(𝑭)≠0𝝀,\operatorname{mult}(P)=\boldsymbol{\mu}\ \ \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \ \ \boldsymbol{\bar{\mu}}=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\mathcal{M}(n)\\ R_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}(\boldsymbol{F})\neq 0\end{subarray}}\boldsymbol{\lambda},

where max\max is w.r.t. the lexicographical ordering.

6.2 The discriminant sequence of a univariate polynomial

In [15], Yang et al. proposed a method for determining the number of distinct real/imaginary roots for univariate polynomials with parametric coefficients. In this subsection, we give a brief review on the work.

Definition 29 (Discrimination matrix).

Given a polynomial

P⁡(x)=an​xn+an−1​xn−1+⋯+a1​x+a0,P(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{1}x+a_{0},

we write the derivative of P⁡(x)P(x) as

P′​(x)=0⋅xn+n​an​xn−1+(n−1)​an−1​xn−2+⋯+a1.P^{\prime}(x)=0\cdot x^{n}+na_{n}x^{n-1}+(n-1)a_{n-1}x^{n-2}+\cdots+a_{1}.

Then the Sylvester matrix of P⁡(x)P(x) and P′​(x)P^{\prime}(x),

Syl⁡(P)=[anan−1an−2⋯a0n​an(n−1)​an−1⋯a1anan−1⋯a2a0n​an⋯2​a2a1⋱⋱anan−1⋯a0n​an⋯a1]{\rm Syl}(P)=\begin{bmatrix}a_{n}&a_{n-1}&a_{n-2}&\cdots&a_{0}&&&\\ &na_{n}&(n-1)a_{n-1}&\cdots&a_{1}&&&\\ &a_{n}&a_{n-1}&\cdots&a_{2}&a_{0}&&\\ &&na_{n}&\cdots&2a_{2}&a_{1}&&\\ &&&\ddots&&&\ddots&\\ &&&&a_{n}&a_{n-1}&\cdots&a_{0}\\ &&&&&na_{n}&\cdots&a_{1}\end{bmatrix}

is called the discrimination matrix of P⁡(x)P(x).

Definition 30 (Discriminant sequence).

Let DiD_{i} denote the 2​i×2​i2i\times 2i principal minor of Syl⁡(P){\rm Syl}(P) for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n. Then the nn-tuple

[D1,D2,…,Dn]\left[D_{1},D_{2},\dots,D_{n}\right]

is called the discriminant sequence of P⁡(x)P(x).

In order to determine the number of distinct real/imaginary roots of PP with its discriminant sequence, we recall the concept of revised sign list [15].

Given a sign list [σ1,σ2,…,σn]∈{−1,0,1}n[\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\dots,\sigma_{n}]\in\{-1,0,1\}^{n}, its revised sign list [σ1′,σ2′,…,σn′][\sigma^{\prime}_{1},\sigma^{\prime}_{2},\dots,\sigma^{\prime}_{n}] can be constructed as follows.

  • •

    If [σi,σi+1,…,σi+j][\sigma_{i},\sigma_{i+1},\dots,\sigma_{i+j}] is a section of the given list, where σi≠0\sigma_{i}\neq 0, σi+1=⋯=σi+j−1=0\sigma_{i+1}=\cdots=\sigma_{i+j-1}=0, σi+j≠0\sigma_{i+j}\neq 0, then we replace the section

    [σi+1,σi+2,…,σi+j−1][\sigma_{i+1},\sigma_{i+2},\dots,\sigma_{i+j-1}]

    by

    [−σi,−σi,σi,σi,−σi,−σi,σi,σi,…];[-\sigma_{i},-\sigma_{i},\sigma_{i},\sigma_{i},-\sigma_{i},-\sigma_{i},\sigma_{i},\sigma_{i},\dots];

    i.e. let

    σi+k′=(−1)k+12⋅σi\sigma^{\prime}_{i+k}=(-1)^{\frac{k+1}{2}}\cdot\sigma_{i}

    for k=1,2,…,j−1k=1,2,\dots,j-1.

  • •

    Otherwise, let σi′=σi\sigma^{\prime}_{i}=\sigma_{i}.

Theorem 31.

Given a polynomial P∈ℝ⁡[x]P\in\mathbb{R}[x], let σ\sigma be the sign list of the discriminant sequence of PP and ν\nu be the number of the sign changes of the revised sign list of σ\sigma. Then we have

  • •

    the number of the pairs of distinct conjugate imaginary roots of PP is ν\nu;

  • •

    the number of the distinct real roots of PP equals η−2​ν\eta-2\nu where η\eta is the number of non-vanishing members in the revised sign list of σ\sigma.

6.3 Algorithm

Combining Theorems 16, 28 and 31, we can derive a new necessary and sufficient condition for a polynomial P=∑i=0nai​xiP=\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_{i}x^{i} having a designated complete multiplicity (𝝁𝑹;𝝁𝑰)(\boldsymbol{\mu_{R}};\boldsymbol{\mu_{I}}). This new condition is based on an observation that if rkr_{k} is a root of PP with multiplicity μk\mu_{k}, then it is a root of GiG_{i} with multiplicity max⁡(μk−i,0)\max(\mu_{k}-i,0).

Let 𝝁\boldsymbol{\mu} be the complex multiplicity of PP corresponding to (𝝁𝑹;𝝁𝑰)(\boldsymbol{\mu_{R}};\boldsymbol{\mu_{I}}). By Theorem 31, with the premise mult⁡(P)=𝝁\operatorname{mult}(P)=\boldsymbol{\mu}, GiG_{i} has ν\nu pairs of distinct imaginary roots if and only if

ν=Var⁡(D1​(Gi,Gi′),…,Dμ¯i+1​(Gi,Gi′))\nu={\rm Var}\left(D_{1}(G_{i},G_{i}^{\prime}),\ldots,D_{\bar{\mu}_{i+1}}(G_{i},G_{i}^{\prime})\right)

where G0:=PG_{0}:=P and Var⁡(L)\operatorname{Var}(L) is the short-hand for the number of sign changes for the revised list of the sign list of LL. Therefore, we have

cmult(P)=(𝝁𝑹;𝝁𝑰)⟺\displaystyle\operatorname*{cmult}\left(P\right)=(\boldsymbol{\mu_{R}};\boldsymbol{\mu_{I}})\ \ \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \ \ (⋀𝜸≻𝝁¯𝜸∈ℳ⁡(n)R𝜸​(𝑭)=0)∧R𝝁¯​(𝑭)≠0\displaystyle\left(\bigwedge_{\begin{subarray}{c}\boldsymbol{\gamma}\succ\boldsymbol{\bar{\mu}}\\ \boldsymbol{\gamma}\in\mathcal{M}(n)\end{subarray}}R_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}(\boldsymbol{F})=0\right)\ \ \ \wedge\ \ R_{\boldsymbol{\bar{\mu}}}(\boldsymbol{F})\neq 0
∧\displaystyle\wedge\ (⋀i=0μ1−1Var(D1(Gi,Gi′),…,Dμ¯i+1(Gi,Gi′))=μ¯I,i+1/2)\displaystyle\left(\bigwedge\limits_{i=0}^{\mu_{1}-1}\ \ {\rm Var}\left(D_{1}(G_{i},G_{i}^{\prime}),\ldots,D_{\bar{\mu}_{i+1}}(G_{i},G_{i}^{\prime})\right)=\bar{\mu}_{I,i+1}/2\right) (14)

where μ¯I,i\bar{\mu}_{I,i} is the ii-th element of 𝝁¯𝑰\boldsymbol{\bar{\mu}_{I}}.

Now we propose the following algorithm as a solution to Problem 5.

Remark 32.

In [15], Yang et al. proposed a method for discriminating the complete multiplicities of a parametric univariate polynomial by counting the numbers of distinct real/imaginary roots of the repeated gcds (called multiple factors there) of the given polynomials. In the 𝖯𝖺𝗋𝖺𝗆𝖾𝗍𝗋𝗂𝖼𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗍𝖾𝖬𝗎𝗅𝗍𝗂𝗉𝗅𝗂𝖼𝗂𝗍𝗒{\sf ParametricCompleteMultiplicity} algorithm, we use the incremental gcds of 𝑭=(P(0),P(1),…,P(n))\boldsymbol{F}=(P^{(0)},P^{(1)},\ldots,P^{(n)}) instead of repeated gcds. Their equivalence seems to be quite straightforward. However, we could not find a reference for its proof and thereby we provide a detailed one in Appendix B for readers’ reference (see Lemma 39).

7 Comparison

In this section, we compare the “sizes” of the conditions generated by the Algorithm ParametricCompleteMultiplicity and those by [15] (abbreviated as YHZ’s method).

7.1 Review on YHZ’s condition

We start by reproducing the result given by YHZ’s method for readers’ convenience.

Assume PP is of degree nn with the complete multiplicity 𝝁𝒄=(𝝁𝑹;𝝁𝑰)\boldsymbol{\mu_{c}}=(\boldsymbol{\mu_{R}};\boldsymbol{\mu_{I}}). Let 𝝁\boldsymbol{\mu} be the complex multiplicity of PP. For the sake of simplicity, we introduce the following shorthand notations.

    si=∑k=i+1μ1μ¯ks_{i}=\sum\limits_{k=i+1}^{\mu_{1}}\bar{\mu}_{k}, i,e., sis_{i} is the degree of G~i\tilde{G}_{i} in xx;

    Let Rk​(G~i,G~i′)¯\overline{R_{k}\left(\tilde{G}_{i},\tilde{G}^{\prime}_{i}\right)} represent the principal coefficient of Rk​(G~i,G~i′)R_{k}\left(\tilde{G}_{i},\tilde{G}^{\prime}_{i}\right), that is, the coefficient of the term xsi−kx^{s_{i}-k} in Rk​(G~i,G~i′)R_{k}\left(\tilde{G}_{i},\tilde{G}^{\prime}_{i}\right).

cmult(P)=(𝝁𝑹;𝝁𝑰)\displaystyle\operatorname*{cmult}\left(P\right)=(\boldsymbol{\mu_{R}};\boldsymbol{\mu_{I}})
⟺\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\ \ \ (⋀i=0μ1−2⋀j=μ¯i+1+1siDj(G~i,G~i′)=0)∧Dsμ1−1​(G~μ1−1,G~μ1−1′)≠0\displaystyle\left(\bigwedge\limits_{i=0}^{\mu_{1}-2}\ \ \bigwedge\limits_{j=\bar{\mu}_{i+1}+1}^{s_{i}}D_{j}(\tilde{G}_{i},\tilde{G}_{i}^{\prime})=0\right)\ \ \ \wedge\ \ D_{s_{\mu_{1}-1}\left(\tilde{G}_{\mu_{1}-1},\tilde{G}_{\mu_{1}-1}^{\prime}\right)}\neq 0

We will assume that ∀𝛍∈ℳ⁡(n)\forall\,\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(n), Rsi​(G~i,G~i′)¯\overline{R_{s_{i}}\left(\tilde{G}_{i},\tilde{G}_{i}^{\prime}\right)} in the above YHZ’s condition is not identically 00 as a polynomial in terms of the coefficients of PP.

7.2 Comparison

We compare the “sizes” of the polynomial conditions generated by the 𝖯𝖺𝗋𝖺𝗆𝖾𝗍𝗋𝗂𝖼𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗍𝖾𝖬𝗎𝗅𝗍𝗂𝗉𝗅𝗂𝖼𝗂𝗍𝗒{\sf ParametricCompleteMultiplicity} algorithm and those given by YHZ’s method from the following two aspects:

  • •

    the numbers of polynomials for partitioning the parameter set, and

  • •

    the degrees of polynomials appearing in the conditions.

Furthermore, we compare the computational efficiency of the two methods via practical examples.

7.2.1 Comparison on the number of polynomials

For simplicity, we introduce the following notations:

  • •

    TYHZ​(n)T_{\rm YHZ}(n): the number of polynomials appearing in YHZ’s condition;

  • •

    TQXY​(n)T_{\rm QXY}(n): the number of polynomials appearing in the new condition (produced by Algorithm 1).

As usual, we assume PP to be a univariate polynomial of degree n≥2n\geq 2 with formal coefficients.

We start by deducing a recursive formula for computing TYHZ​(n)T_{\rm YHZ}(n). In YHZ’s method, the main idea is to restore the complete multiplicity of PP by counting the number of distinct real/imaginary roots of G~0,…,G~n−1\tilde{G}_{0},\ldots,\tilde{G}_{n-1}. Thus one only needs to discriminate the cases when G~i\tilde{G}_{i} has different numbers of distinct real roots/pairs of imaginary roots. For this purpose, only the polynomials in the discriminant sequence of G~i\tilde{G}_{i}’s are needed.

In the first step, we compute all the potential gcds of G0~\tilde{G_{0}} and G~0′\tilde{G}_{0}^{\prime}, i.e., Rn​(G~0,G~0′)R_{n}(\tilde{G}_{0},\tilde{G}_{0}^{\prime}), …, R1​(G~0,G~0′)R_{1}(\tilde{G}_{0},\tilde{G}_{0}^{\prime}). We also need D1​(G~0,G~0′),…,Dn​(G~0,G~0′)D_{1}(\tilde{G}_{0},\tilde{G}_{0}^{\prime}),\ldots,D_{n}(\tilde{G}_{0},\tilde{G}_{0}^{\prime}) to discriminate the numbers of real roots/pairs of imaginary roots G~0\tilde{G}_{0} may have. In this step, we need nn polynomials in the parameters. Note that each Ri​(G~0,G~0′)R_{i}(\tilde{G}_{0},\tilde{G}_{0}^{\prime}) is a potential gcd of G~0\tilde{G}_{0} and G~0′\tilde{G}_{0}^{\prime} with degree n−in-i where i=1,…,n−1i=1,\ldots,n-1. When i=n−1i=n-1, deg⁡Ri​(G~0,G~0′)=1\deg R_{i}(\tilde{G}_{0},\tilde{G}_{0}^{\prime})=1. We immediately know that Ri​(G~0,G~0′)R_{i}(\tilde{G}_{0},\tilde{G}_{0}^{\prime}) has only one (real) root and there are no other cases to be discriminated. So we do not need extra polynomials. On the other hand, to discriminate all the complete multiplicities of G~i\tilde{G}_{i}, we need TYHZ​(n−i)T_{\rm YHZ}(n-i) polynomials. As a result, when n≥2n\geq 2, we have

TYHZ​(n)=n+∑i=1n−2TYHZ​(n−i)=n+∑i=2n−1TYHZ​(i)T_{\rm YHZ}(n)=n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-2}T_{\rm YHZ}(n-i)=n+\sum_{i=2}^{n-1}T_{\rm YHZ}(i)

One can easily derive from the relation that when n≥3n\geq 3,

TYHZ​(n)−TYHZ​(n−1)=1+TYHZ​(n−1)T_{\rm YHZ}(n)-T_{\rm YHZ}(n-1)=1+T_{\rm YHZ}(n-1)

Therefore,

TYHZ​(n)=34⋅2n−1T_{\rm YHZ}(n)=\frac{3}{4}\cdot 2^{n}-1

Now we consider the number of polynomials required by the new method to discriminate all the complete multiplicities of PP, which is denoted by TQXY​(n)T_{\rm QXY}(n). To discriminant all the complex multiplicities of PP, we need R𝝁R_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}’s where 𝝁∈ℳ⁡(n)\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(n) and the total number of R𝝁R_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}’s is #​ℳ​(n)\#\mathcal{M}(n). To discriminate all the complete multiplicities of PP, we need to consider all the possibilities of GiG_{i}, which form a set {R𝜹:𝜹∈𝒩⁡(n)}\{R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}:\boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathcal{N}(n)\} by Theorem 16 with

𝒩(n)={(δ1,…,δt):δ1+⋯+δt<n,δ1≥…≥δt≥1}.\mathcal{N}(n)=\left\{(\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{t}):\,\delta_{1}+\cdots+\delta_{t}<n,\delta_{1}\geq\ldots\geq\delta_{t}\geq 1\right\}.

Since 𝒩⁡(n)=⋃i=0n−1ℳ⁡(i)\mathcal{N}(n)=\bigcup_{i=0}^{n-1}\mathcal{M}(i), we have

{R𝜹:𝜹∈𝒩⁡(n)}=⋃i=0n−1{R𝜹:𝜹∈ℳ⁡(i)}.\{R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}:\boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathcal{N}(n)\}=\bigcup_{i=0}^{n-1}\{R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}:\boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathcal{M}(i)\}.

In each subset of the right-hand side, R𝜹R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}’s have the same degree n−in-i. When i=n−1i=n-1, R𝜹R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}’s are of degree 11 and we will not add any polynomial to the condition. When 0≤i≤n−20\leq i\leq n-2, to discriminate all the possible numbers of distinct real/imaginary roots for each R𝜹R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}, we need D1​(R𝜹′),R𝜹,…,Dn−i​(R𝜹,R𝜹′)D_{1}(R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{\prime}),R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}},\ldots,D_{n-i}(R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}},R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{\prime}) and thus altogether #​ℳ​(i)⋅(n−i)\#\mathcal{M}(i)\cdot(n-i) polynomials are required to discriminate the numbers of distinct real/imaginary roots for all R𝜹R_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}’s of degree n−in-i. In summary, in the condition generated by the proposed method, the number of polynomials is

TQXY​(n)=#​ℳ​(n)+∑i=0n−2#​ℳ​(i)⋅(n−i)T_{\rm QXY}(n)=\#\mathcal{M}(n)+\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}\#\mathcal{M}(i)\cdot(n-i)

In Table 1, we list the two numbers, i.e., TYHZT_{\rm YHZ} and TQXYT_{\rm QXY}, for n=3,…,18n=3,\ldots,18. In Figure 1, we show the trend of the two numbers as nn increases. It is observed that

  • •

    As expected, TYHZT_{\rm YHZ} increases exponentially with nn while TQXYT_{\rm QXY} is not. In fact, it is seen from Figure 1(a) that TQXYT_{\rm QXY} increases significantly slower than TYHZT_{\rm YHZ} as nn increases.

  • •

    From Fig. 1(b), we can further see that the ratio of TYHZT_{\rm YHZ} to TQXYT_{\rm QXY} is always greater than 11 for n≥7n\geq 7, which indicates that TQXY<TYHZT_{\rm QXY}<T_{\rm YHZ} when n≥7n\geq 7.

  • •

    Moreover, Fig. 1(b) exhibits an exponential increase on the ratio TYHZ/TQXYT_{\rm YHZ}/T_{\rm QXY} along with nn. Thus, TYHZT_{\rm YHZ} becomes dramatically smaller than TYHZT_{\rm YHZ} when nn grows.

7.2.2 Comparison on the degree of polynomials

    dYHZd_{\text{YHZ}}: the maximal degree of polynomials appearing in YHZ’s condition;

  • •

    dQXYd_{\text{QXY}}: the maximal degree of polynomials appearing in the new condition (produced by Algorithm 1).

From Propositions 35 and 36, it is immediately seen that the maximal degree of polynomials in the condition given by YHZ’s method increases in exponential scale w.r.t. nn while that given by QXY’s method shows an increase in polynomial scale. Furthermore, with the help of Propositions 35 and 36, one can easily show the following proposition.

Proposition 37.

When n≥8n\geq 8, dYHZ≥dQXYd_{\rm YHZ}\geq d_{\rm QXY}.

In Table 2, we list the two numbers, i.e., dYHZd_{\rm YHZ} and dQXYd_{\rm QXY}, for n=3,…,8,n=3,\ldots,8, while Fig. 3 shows the trend of the two numbers as nn increases. From Table 2 and Fig. 3, we make the following observations.

  • •

    When d<6d<6, dYHZ≤dQXYd_{\rm YHZ}\leq d_{\rm QXY} and their differences is relatively small (no more than 2, see Table 2). Roughly speaking, dQXY≈dYHZd_{\rm QXY}\approx d_{\rm YHZ}.

  • •

    When nn surpasses 66, dQXYd_{\rm QXY} is significantly smaller than dYHZd_{\rm YHZ} (see Fig. 3(a)). When n≥4n\geq 4, the ratio dYHZdQXY\dfrac{d_{\rm YHZ}}{d_{\rm QXY}} grows as nn increases (see Fig. 3(b)). Therefore, the size of the polynomial with the maximal degree in YHZ’s method becomes even bigger than that in the proposed method. Hence, it is expected that when nn is large enough, the new method will be far more efficient than YHZ’s method.

7.2.3 Comparison on performance

In this part, we compare YHZ’s method to the proposed method (i.e., QXY’s method) in terms of computational efficiency. For this purpose, we carry out several experiments for nn ranging from 33 to 99. The experiments are performed on a PC equipped with an Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-7300U processor and an 8GB RAM.

The experimental results are reported in Table 3 where tYHZt_{\text{YHZ}} and tQXYt_{\text{QXY}} represent the time cost (in seconds) charged by YHZ’s method and the proposed method, respectively. It is seen that the proposed method outperforms YHZ’s method when solving relatively larger examples (see n=7,8n=7,8 in Table 3).

Although both methods fail on the case n=9n=9, the new algorithm can still give some positive results. For example, if we take the polynomial of the following form

P=x9+a7​x7+⋯+a0P=x^{9}+a_{7}x^{7}+\cdots+a_{0}

(which can also be viewed as a generic form of polynomials with degree 99) as input, the algorithm ParametricCompleteMultiplicity succeeds after 3009.296 seconds (<1<1 hour) while YHZ’s method does not terminate after running for 10 hours.

8 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose a new algorithm for solving the parametric complete multiplicity problem. Different from using the repeated gcd computation in the classical one [15], the new approach uses incremental gcds instead, which can effectively reduce the size of the polynomials appearing in the condition.

It is noted that in the new approach, we also confront with nested determinants/subresultants, which requires intensive computation. Thus a natural question is: is it possible to use non-nested determinants to solve the parametric complete multiplicity problem? The investigation along this direction is very attractive not only because it can help to improve the efficiency of the algorithms but also provides a closed form for the parametric complete multiplicity problem. Another interesting direction is to explore the hidden structures for subresultant used in the algorithm 𝖯𝖺𝗋𝖺𝗆𝖾𝗍𝗋𝗂𝖼𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗍𝖾𝖬𝗎𝗅𝗍𝗂𝗉𝗅𝗂𝖼𝗂𝗍𝗒{\sf ParametricCompleteMultiplicity} which may further enhance the computational efficiency.

Appendix B.

Given a polynomial PP, the repeated gcd of PP and P′P^{\prime} is defined as (G~1,…,G~n)(\tilde{G}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{G}_{n}) where

G~i=gcd⁡(G~i−1,G~i−1′)\tilde{G}_{i}=\gcd(\tilde{G}_{i-1},\tilde{G}^{\prime}_{i-1})

with G~0:=P\tilde{G}_{0}:=P. In this paper, we use the incremental gcds of P(0),P(1),…P^{(0)},P^{(1)},\ldots instead of repeated gcds. In the appendix, we provide a detailed proof on their equivalence.

Lemma 39.

Let G0=PG_{0}=P. Then for i≥0i\geq 0, we have Gi∼G~iG_{i}\sim\tilde{G}_{i}.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, we assume

P=an​∏k=1m(x−rk)μk.P=a_{n}\prod_{k=1}^{m}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}}.

To prove Gi∼G~iG_{i}\sim\tilde{G}_{i}, we only need to show

  • •

    Gi∼∏μk>i(x−rk)μk−iG_{i}\sim\prod_{\mu_{k}>i}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-i}, and

  • •

    G~i∼∏μk>i(x−rk)μk−i,\tilde{G}_{i}\sim\prod_{\mu_{k}>i}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-i},

whose proof will be given in an inductive manner.

Base case. When i=0i=0, we have

G0=G~0=P=an​∏μk>0(x−rk)μkG_{0}=\tilde{G}_{0}=P=a_{n}\prod_{\mu_{k}>0}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}}

which is obviously true.

Induction step. We assume the claim holds when i=ji=j, i.e.

Gj\displaystyle G_{j} =gcd⁡(Gj−1,P(j))∼∏μk>j(x−rk)μk−j,\displaystyle=\gcd(G_{j-1},P^{(j)})\sim\prod_{\mu_{k}>j}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j},
G~j\displaystyle\tilde{G}_{j} =gcd⁡(G~j−1,G~j−1′)∼∏μk>j(x−rk)μk−j.\displaystyle=\gcd(\tilde{G}_{j-1},\tilde{G}^{\prime}_{j-1})\sim\prod_{\mu_{k}>j}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j}.

Then for i=j+1i=j+1,

Gj+1=gcd⁡(Gj,P(j+1)),G~j+1=gcd⁡(G~j,G~j′).G_{j+1}=\gcd(G_{j},P^{(j+1)}),\qquad\tilde{G}_{j+1}=\gcd(\tilde{G}_{j},\tilde{G}^{\prime}_{j}).

Next we deduce the expressions for Gj+1G_{j+1} and G~j+1\tilde{G}_{j+1}, respectively.

By assumption, Gj∼∏μk>j(x−rk)μk−jG_{j}\sim\prod_{\mu_{k}>j}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j}. Obviously, we have

  • •

    ∏μk>j+1(x−rk)μk−(j+1)|Gj\prod_{\mu_{k}>j+1}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-(j+1)}\mid G_{j}, and

  • •

    when μk>j\mu_{k}>j,

    (x−rk)μk|P(0),(x−rk)μk−1|P(1),…,(x−rk)μk−j|P(j)(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}}\mid P^{(0)},(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-1}\mid P^{(1)},\ldots,(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j}\mid P^{(j)}

Next we show that ∏μk>j+1(x−rk)μk−(j+1)|P(j+1)\prod_{\mu_{k}>j+1}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-(j+1)}\mid P^{(j+1)}. The key for verifying the claim is the observation that when μk>j+1\mu_{k}>j+1,

P(j+1)​(rk)=⋯=P(μk−1)​(rk)=0,P^{(j+1)}(r_{k})=\cdots=P^{(\mu_{k}-1)}(r_{k})=0,

but P(μk)​(rk)≠0P^{(\mu_{k})}(r_{k})\neq 0, which indicates that x=rkx=r_{k} is the multiple roots of P(j+1)​(x)P^{(j+1)}(x) with multiplicity μk−(j+1)\mu_{k}-(j+1). Thereby, (x−rk)μk−(j+1)|P(j+1)​(x)(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-(j+1)}\mid P^{(j+1)}(x). Moreover, we also have (x−rk)μk−j∤P(j+1)(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j}\nmid P^{(j+1)}. Hence

Gj+1=gcd⁡(Gj,P(j+1))∼∏μk>j+1(x−rk)μk−(j+1)G_{j+1}=\gcd(G_{j},P^{(j+1)})\sim\prod_{\mu_{k}>j+1}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-(j+1)}

Again, by assumption, G~j∼∏μk>j(x−rk)μk−j\tilde{G}_{j}\sim\prod_{\mu_{k}>j}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j}. Thus

G~j′∼(∏μk>j(x−rk)μk−j)′\displaystyle\tilde{G}^{\prime}_{j}\sim\left(\prod_{\mu_{k}>j}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j}\right)^{\prime} =∑μk>j((μk−j)​(x−rk)μk−j−1​∏ℓ≠kμℓ>j(x−rℓ)μℓ−j)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu_{k}>j}\left((\mu_{k}-j)(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j-1}\prod_{\underset{\mu_{\ell}>j}{\ell\neq k}}(x-r_{\ell})^{\mu_{\ell}-j}\right)
=(∑μk>j(μk−j)​∏ℓ≠kμℓ>j(x−rℓ))​(∏μk>j(x−rk)μk−j−1).\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{\mu_{k}>j}(\mu_{k}-j)\prod_{\underset{\mu_{\ell}>j}{\ell\neq k}}(x-r_{\ell})\right)\left(\prod_{\mu_{k}>j}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j-1}\right).

∼gcd⁡(∏μk>j(x−rk)μk−j,(∏μk>j(x−rk)μk−j)′)\displaystyle\sim\gcd\left(\prod_{\mu_{k}>j}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j},\left(\prod_{\mu_{k}>j}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j}\right)^{\prime}\right)
=gcd⁡(∏μk>j(x−rk)μk−j,(∑μk>j(μk−j)​∏ℓ≠kμℓ>j(x−rℓ))​(∏μk>j(x−rk)μk−j−1))\displaystyle=\gcd\left(\prod_{\mu_{k}>j}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j},\left(\sum_{\mu_{k}>j}(\mu_{k}-j)\prod_{\underset{\mu_{\ell}>j}{\ell\neq k}}(x-r_{\ell})\right)\left(\prod_{\mu_{k}>j}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j-1}\right)\right)
=gcd⁡(∏μk>j(x−rk),∑μk>j(μk−j)​∏ℓ≠kμℓ>j(x−rℓ))⋅(∏μk>j(x−rk)μk−j−1).\displaystyle=\gcd\left(\prod_{\mu_{k}>j}(x-r_{k}),\sum_{\mu_{k}>j}(\mu_{k}-j)\prod_{\underset{\mu_{\ell}>j}{\ell\neq k}}(x-r_{\ell})\right)\cdot\left(\prod_{\mu_{k}>j}(x-r_{k})^{\mu_{k}-j-1}\right).

It remains to show that

which can be proved with the following verification

for u∈{μk:μk>j}u\in\{\mu_{k}:\,\mu_{k}>j\}. Hence
